practiceSet.title: U8.LT4 Practice: Kingdom Fungi
practiceSet.description: Practice describing fungi: the 4 main characteristics, how they differ from plants, hyphae and mycelium, how they feed and reproduce with spores, the 4 groups, lichens, and how fungi help and harm us.

activity.title: U8.LT4 Relearning: Kingdom Fungi
activity.content:
**What you need to be able to do:** I can give a general description of the organisms in the Kingdom Fungi.

**Think of an iceberg.** The part of an iceberg you see above the water is tiny compared to what's hidden below. A mushroom is the tip of the iceberg. The real, living body of the fungus is a huge network of threads hidden in the soil or wood, and the mushroom is just the "fruit" that pops up to release spores.

**Mycology** is the study of fungi (fungus = one, fungi = more than one).

**4 main characteristics of fungi:** (1) They are **eukaryotic** (their cells have nuclei). (2) They are **heterotrophs**: they depend on other organisms for food. (3) **Most are multicellular; some are unicellular** (yeast). (4) They are **classified by the way they reproduce**.

**4 reasons fungi are different from plants:** fungi (1) **lack chlorophyll**, (2) are **not photosynthetic**, so they can't make their own food, (3) **never reproduce by seeds**, and (4) have cell walls made of **chitin** (plant cell walls are cellulose).

**How fungi feed.** Most fungi are **saprophytes** that feed on dead or decaying organisms; some are **parasites**. Their hyphae grow into the food, release enzymes that break it down, and then **absorb** the nutrients. That makes fungi **major decomposers** that recycle nutrients back into the soil.

**Parts of a fungus.** **Hyphae** (one is a hypha) are thin, thread-like structures that form the body. A **mycelium** is a mass of hyphae, usually hidden in soil, wood, or food. A **germ tube** is the first hypha growing out of a spore. The part we see (like a mushroom) is the **fruiting body**, which carries out reproduction.

**The 4 groups (phyla):**
- **Zygomycota, common molds:** bread mold; spores are made in **sporangia** on the tips of hyphae.
- **Ascomycota, sac fungi:** spores are made in sacs; yeast, morels, truffles, the fungus in lichens, and many plant diseases (Dutch elm disease, oak wilt).
- **Basidiomycota, club fungi:** mushrooms, shelf fungi, puffballs; spores are made on the ends of clubs.
- **Imperfect fungi:** only reproduce **asexually**; cause most fungal diseases in humans (yeast infection, athlete's foot, ringworm); **Penicillium** is the source of the antibiotic penicillin.

**Reproduction.** Most fungi reproduce with microscopic **spores**. Reproduction is classified by the way the spores form and the **shape** of the structure that makes them. Most fungi don't grow tall enough to get above the still air near the ground, so they **shoot their spores** or use **wind, water, or animals**. Pieces of hyphae can also grow into new fungi if there is enough moisture and food.

**Lichens** are a partnership between a fungus and a photosynthetic partner (green algae or cyanobacteria): the partner makes food, and the fungus gives protection and support.

**Good and bad.** Helpful: decomposers, antibiotics (Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928), and foods (yeast for bread, mushrooms, morels, truffles). Harmful: human diseases (athlete's foot, ringworm, yeast infections), crop and tree diseases, food spoilage, and poisonous mushrooms.

**Worked example 1:** A forgotten orange grows a fuzzy blue-green coat made of tiny threads. The coat has no chlorophyll and puffs out powdery spores. Which kingdom? Step 1: No chlorophyll means it can't be a plant. Step 2: The threads are hyphae, and feeding on old fruit makes it a saprophyte. Step 3: Hyphae plus spores fit fungi. **Answer:** Kingdom Fungi (this one is Penicillium).

**Worked example 2:** A hard, shelf-like growth sticks out from the trunk of a dead tree. Its underside releases spores. Which group? Step 1: It grows on dead wood and has no chlorophyll, so it is a fungus. Step 2: Shelf fungi make their spores on the ends of tiny club-shaped structures on the underside. Step 3: Spores on clubs means club fungi. **Answer:** Basidiomycota (club fungi).

**Worked example 3:** A circle of mushrooms (a "fairy ring") shows up on a lawn, and the next year the circle is wider. Why a ring? Step 1: One mycelium spreads outward underground from where a spore first landed. Step 2: The newest, most active hyphae are at the outer edge. Step 3: That edge pushes up mushrooms, the fruiting bodies. **Answer:** the ring marks the edge of one growing mycelium; the mushrooms are just its fruit.

**Watch out for:** calling fungi plants (no chlorophyll, chitin walls, no seeds); saying fungi make their own food; thinking the mushroom is the whole fungus; mixing up hyphae (the threads) and mycelium (the mass of threads); and thinking ringworm is caused by a worm.
prompts: List the 4 main characteristics of fungi and the 4 reasons fungi are different from plants.
Define hyphae and mycelium, and explain how a fungus gets its food from a rotting log.
Make a table of the 4 groups of fungi. For each, tell how it reproduces or makes spores, and give one example.
Explain what a lichen is and what each partner gives the other.
Give two ways fungi help people and two ways fungi harm people, plants, or food.
